title: SFTP
summary: SFTP is a binary file protocol tunneled as an SSH subsystem over one encrypted TCP connection — precise mechanism, trade-offs, failures, and interview use.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: **SFTP is not FTP with encryption bolted on. It is a completely different binary packet protocol executed inside an SSH session over a single TCP connection.** That one choice explains its firewall-friendliness, its security properties, and why it will never match object storage on throughput.

SFTP — SSH File Transfer Protocol — is a stateful, binary request-response protocol for file operations: open, read, write, close, stat, mkdir, rename, remove, list. Every message is framed as a length-prefixed packet with type, request ID, handle or path, and status code. It has no notion of ASCII commands, data ports, or directory listing text to parse. The client opens file handles on the server and issues offset-based reads and writes against those handles, much like a remote system-call interface. That is why SFTP can resume, do random access, and atomically rename — it models files, not a byte stream.

Transport is SSH, almost always TCP port 22. Authentication, key exchange, encryption, integrity, channel multiplexing, and the file protocol itself all share that one connection. The server does not speak SFTP until the client has completed SSH transport setup, proven server identity via host key, authenticated the user, opened a channel, and requested the `sftp` subsystem. Only then does the file packet loop start. This layering is deliberate: SFTP inherits confidentiality, integrity, server authentication, and user authentication from SSH instead of reimplementing them.

The single-connection design is the core trade-off. FTP uses a control connection plus a new data connection per transfer, often with active-mode callbacks that die behind NAT. FTPS wraps that mess in TLS and still needs a range of passive ports opened through every firewall. SFTP multiplexes everything over one outbound TCP flow. The operational win is enormous: one port to allow, one flow to audit, one TLS-style upgrade path to manage. The price is fate-sharing — command latency, bulk throughput, rekey stalls, and flow-control backpressure all contend on the same connection.

SSH is three layered protocols stacked on TCP. The transport layer negotiates ciphers, MACs, compression, and host-key algorithm, performs Diffie-Hellman key exchange, verifies the server host key, and derives symmetric session keys. From that point every byte is encrypted and integrity-protected. The authentication layer then proves who the user is — password, publickey, keyboard-interactive, or multi-factor chained together. Only after success does the connection layer allow channels: logical streams multiplexed by channel ID with per-channel windowing. SFTP is just one channel type that execs a subsystem, alongside shell, exec, and port-forwarding channels that could share the same SSH session.

blocks.title: SFTP session establishment
blocks.caption: SSH transport, auth, then SFTP subsystem — no file bytes move until the last step.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A[Client TCP connect port 22] --> B[SSH version string exchange]
  B --> C[Algorithm negotiation and DH key exchange]
  C --> D[Verify server host key and derive session keys]
  D --> E[Encrypted tunnel up all further traffic protected]
  E --> F[User authentication password or publickey]
  F --> G[Open channel and request sftp subsystem]
  G --> H[Binary packet loop OPEN READ WRITE CLOSE]
  H --> I[Rekey or disconnect]

blocks.text: Once the subsystem is active, the protocol is strictly packetized. The client sends `SSH_FXP_INIT` with its version, the server answers `SSH_FXP_VERSION`, and then every operation carries a monotonically increasing request ID so responses can be matched out of order. `OPEN` returns an opaque handle, `READ` and `WRITE` specify handle plus offset plus length, `CLOSE` releases the handle. Attributes — size, uid, gid, permissions, timestamps — travel as typed flags, not as `ls -l` text. The reason this matters for design interviews: the server is stateful per handle and per session. Disconnect and your handles die. Concurrent writes to the same offset are last-writer-wins unless the application adds locking. There is no built-in distributed consistency, no conditional write, no atomic append.

blocks.title: SFTP channel lifecycle
blocks.caption: Stateful handles and periodic rekey explain most production stalls.
blocks.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Connected
  Connected --> Authenticated: user auth succeeds
  Authenticated --> SubsystemActive: start sftp subsystem
  SubsystemActive --> Transferring: OPEN handle READ WRITE
  Transferring --> SubsystemActive: CLOSE handle
  SubsystemActive --> Rekeying: KEXINIT by time or bytes
  Rekeying --> SubsystemActive: new keys installed
  SubsystemActive --> Closed: disconnect
  Transferring --> Closed: TCP reset

blocks.caption: What SFTP buys you and what it charges you — no free properties.
rows: Single TCP connection
One firewall rule, NAT-friendly, trivial to audit and allowlist
Head-of-line blocking: one lossy path stalls commands and data together
SSH encryption + integrity
Confidentiality and tamper detection without separate certificates
CPU per byte for cipher and MAC, plus throughput collapse on high-latency links
Host-key + user auth model
Mutual authentication with keys, passwords, or MFA chaining
Key distribution and rotation burden; host-key change looks identical to attack
Binary packet protocol
Reliable random access, resume, rename, typed attributes
Chatty round trips per block; small reads amplify latency
Stateful handles
POSIX-like semantics clients understand
Server must track state; crash or load-balancer shift loses handles
Ubiquitous SSH servers
No extra daemon, works anywhere SSH works
Couples file-transfer load and blast radius to shell-access infrastructure

blocks.text: Why it is shaped this way

SFTP exists because FTP's two-connection architecture is unsecurable and unmanageable through modern networks. Fixing FTP meant fixing port negotiation, separate data-channel encryption, credential exposure, and text parsing — essentially redesigning it. Reusing SSH solved authentication and encryption in one stroke and gave operators a daemon they already hardened. The trade-off chosen was correctness and deployability over raw speed. Multiplexing with per-channel windowing keeps the protocol simple and ordered, but it means SFTP never learned parallel striping, checksum-offloaded streaming, or zero-copy object semantics. That is why a tuned HTTPS download from object storage will beat SFTP by 5-10x on the same network: fewer round trips, larger segments, CDN parallelism, no per-packet cipher window to drain.

blocks.title: Throughput is window-limited, not bandwidth-limited
blocks.text: Default SFTP read sizes of 32 KB with one outstanding request turn a 100 ms link into ~300 KB/s no matter how fat the pipe is. If you need speed, you need concurrent outstanding reads, larger buffers, or pipelining — and you must say so in the interview before anyone believes your migration plan.

SFTP failures are deceptive because SSH masks them as generic disconnects. The three dominant classes are auth and key failures, middlebox and window stalls, and state and filesystem impedance mismatches. Host-key rotation without client pinning update produces `host key verification failed` across an entire fleet at 3 AM. Rekey by bytes or time pauses the channel while new keys are derived, which shows up as periodic multi-second stalls on long transfers. Idle NAT timeouts silently drop the single TCP flow, so the client hangs in `READ` waiting for a response ID that will never arrive. On the server side, `chroot` jails, forced commands, and umask mismatches produce the classic symptom: login succeeds, `PUT` fails with permission denied, and everyone blames the network.

blocks.caption: Failure signatures you should recognize without logs.
rows: Host-key mismatch
All clients reject connection immediately after server rebuild
New host key not distributed; client correctly treats it as impersonation
Auth succeeds, subsystem fails
`Permission denied` or `subsystem request failed` right after login
User shell set to nologin without internal-sftp, or chroot ownership wrong
Periodic stall every N GB
Throughput drops to zero for 2-10s then resumes
SSH rekey by traffic; single connection blocks data during KEX
Hang on large files over WAN
Fast start then freeze, eventually timeout
TCP window plus SFTP window exhaustion; tiny outstanding request count
Idle disconnect behind NAT
Overnight batch jobs die with `Connection reset`
Stateful firewall drops idle flow; no keepalive configured
Partial file visible to consumer
Downstream job reads truncated file
Writer uploads directly to final name; no temp-file plus atomic rename

blocks.text: The partial-file problem deserves special attention because it is an application bug, not a protocol bug. SFTP has no atomic publish primitive visible to pollers. A consumer scanning a directory will see a file the moment `OPEN` creates it, long before `CLOSE` finishes. The fix is convention, not configuration: write to a staging name or staging directory, then `RENAME` to the pickup path. Rename over the same filesystem is atomic and becomes your commit point. Add idempotent consumers that handle redelivery, because at-least-once delivery plus retry is the only sane contract over a stateful protocol that loses handles on disconnect.

blocks.code:
Port 22
Protocol 2
Subsystem sftp internal-sftp

Match Group sftp-only
    ChrootDirectory /srv/sftp/%u
    ForceCommand internal-sftp -u 0027
    AllowTcpForwarding no
    X11Forwarding no
    PasswordAuthentication no
    # root must own chroot path; writable subdir inside
    # mkdir -p /srv/sftp/alice/incoming && chown alice:sftp-only incoming

ClientAliveInterval 30
ClientAliveCountMax 3
MaxSessions 50
MaxStartups 20:30:100

import paramiko

ssh = paramiko.SSHClient()
ssh.load_system_host_keys()  # fail closed on unknown host key
ssh.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.RejectPolicy())
ssh.connect("sftp.example", username="batch", key_filename="/keys/batch_ed25519",
            look_for_keys=False, allow_agent=False, timeout=10)

# Trade-off: more prefetch = higher WAN throughput, more memory + rework on abort
sftp = ssh.open_sftp()
sftp.get_channel().settimeout(30)
with sftp.open("/incoming/ledger.csv", "rb") as remote:
    remote.prefetch(1024 * 1024)  # keep multiple READs in flight
    while True:
        chunk = remote.read(256 * 1024)
        if not chunk:
            break
        process(chunk)
# Publish pattern: upload tmp then rename — never poll a growing file
sftp.put("/local/out.csv", "/incoming/out.csv.tmp")
sftp.rename("/incoming/out.csv.tmp", "/incoming/out.csv")

blocks.text: How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Design partner file ingestion over SFTP
items.text: Clarify volume, file sizes, frequency, and who owns keys. Propose chrooted service accounts per partner, staging plus atomic rename, poller or notification hook, virus scan and schema validation before promotion. Trade-off: isolation per account costs operational overhead but bounds blast radius.

items.title: Secure it end to end
items.text: Host-key pinning, publickey-only auth, key rotation runbook, IP allowlisting, and audit logging of OPEN, WRITE, RENAME. State what SSH gives you — encryption in flight — and what it does not — no encryption at rest, no non-repudiation of file contents.

items.title: Make it scale and survive failure
items.text: Single SFTP node is stateful and sticky. Scale by sharding partners across nodes or fronting with a managed transfer service backed by object storage. Add keepalives, idempotent consumers, checksum sidecars, and dead-letter quarantine. Name the cost: horizontal scale breaks handle affinity and complicates atomic rename.

items.title: Fix the throughput complaint
items.text: Diagnose window and round-trip limits before adding bandwidth. Increase max packet, enable pipelined concurrent reads, compress only text, avoid cipher downgrade hacks. If the workload is bulk distribution, argue for HTTPS plus signed URLs — SFTP is the wrong tool and saying so scores points.

items.title: Answer the migration trap
items.text: When asked to replace SFTP, do not propose a flag day. Propose dual-publish to SFTP and object storage, checksum parity, then cut consumers over. Partners move slower than code — backwards compatibility is the design constraint.

items: **SFTP and FTPS are the same thing.** They share nothing but the word file. SFTP is an SSH subsystem on one port; FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS on multiple ports. Conflating them signals you have never opened a firewall for either.

**Port 22 means it is SSH shell access.** SFTP can be jailed with `internal-sftp` plus `ForceCommand` so the account can move files and run nothing else. Failing to mention chroot and disabled forwarding looks naive.

**Encryption means integrity and authenticity of files.** SSH protects bytes in flight. It does not prove who authored the file, that it was not replaced at rest, or that the content is well-formed. You still need signatures or checksums and schema validation.

**Keys are automatically secure.** A shared private key emailed to five partners with no rotation is worse than a strong password with MFA. Key lifecycle — issuance, pinning, rotation, revocation — is the actual security design.

**SFTP supports resume and locking natively.** Resume is client-driven re-`OPEN` plus offset `READ`; there is no server-side session resume. There is no cross-client byte-range locking. If two writers race, you get interleaving, not an error.
**Faster network fixes slow SFTP.** On high-latency links throughput is `window / RTT`, not link capacity. Without pipelining and larger outstanding reads, extra bandwidth is invisible.

blocks.text: When to use it, when to kill it

blocks.caption: SFTP is a compatibility choice, not a performance choice.
rows: Bank or vendor mandates batch files over SSH
Use SFTP
Compliance and partner capability outweigh elegance; meet them where they are
Low-volume, human-driven ops and support uploads
Use SFTP
Ubiquitous clients and one firewall rule beat building a portal
High-throughput bulk distribution or global downloads
Avoid — use HTTPS + object storage
CDN caching, range GETs, and parallel streams beat single-connection windows
Event-driven microservice communication
Avoid — use queue + object reference
Polling directories is latent, brittle, and unobservable compared to events
Cross-region large datasets with resume needs
Avoid — use multipart object upload
Native checksums, parallel parts, and stateless retry dominate stateful handles

blocks.text: Choose SFTP when the constraint is organizational, not technical: a partner, auditor, or legacy workflow requires it. In that case isolate it aggressively — dedicated accounts, chroot, no shell, staging plus rename, checksums, and a promotion pipeline that treats every inbound file as hostile until validated. Choose anything else when you control both ends and care about scale, latency, or cost per gigabyte. The senior answer is not to defend SFTP as modern, but to bound it as a hardened edge adapter feeding a sane internal pipeline built on object storage and events.

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: **SFTP is a stateful binary file protocol run as an SSH subsystem over a single encrypted connection — trivial to firewall and secure in flight, but window-limited, sticky, and the wrong default for high-throughput or event-driven transfers.**
